Built toward the wrong place Product Management AI Software Development AI Agent Product Strategy The Fastest Way to Build the Wrong Thing Makssoud Alex 4 min read · Oct 30, 2026 -- Listen Share AI has made execution cheap. That makes our decisions the expensive part. Ask an AI for a product brief and you’ll get one in under a minute. Ask it to turn that brief into a roadmap, then into engineering tickets, then into working code, and it will keep going. Every step looks finished. Every step looks like progress. That’s what worries me a little. Looking finished and being right are two very different things, and AI has become very good at the first one. So here’s the question I keep coming back to: are we accelerating progress, or just accelerating execution? Forty people, vague briefs, and Claude At a recent Shine offsite, my colleague Olivier Chatelin ran an AI workshop for about 40 of us. I helped shape the product side of it and took part in the exercises. The setup was simple. Each team got a deliberately vague product request and had to work with Claude to turn it into something a team could actually build. We gave no ready-made prompts. Teams had to find the right questions themselves, clarify the problem, explore options, pick one, challenge their own assumptions and break the work into tasks. One request read: “I want CPAs to be able to request missing information or documents from their clients while doing accounting work.” It’s one sentence hiding dozens of decisions. Which information? Through which channel? What happens when the client never answers? Two teams received the exact same sentence, on purpose, so we could compare where each one ended up. The first rule fit on a sticky note: Claude asks, humans decide. Before proposing anything, Claude had to ask the five to seven questions that would most change what we should build. Anything a team couldn’t answer had to be written down as an assumption, not quietly filled in. “The two teams with that request ended up designing noticeably different products.” In the debriefs, one question came up again and again: Did we actually make that product decision, or did Claude make it for us? It’s a fair question. AI is remarkably good at filling gaps with plausible answers, and in a room full of busy people, a plausible answer can slip through and quietly become “what we agreed.” What Brooks’s Law has to do with it A few days later I read Jan van den Berg’s article The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI . He revisits Fred Brooks’s old rule: adding people to a late software project makes it later, because every new person adds coordination cost. AI agents remove some of that cost. They don’t need onboarding, and they can work in parallel. But as van den Berg points out, coordination doesn’t disappear. Someone still has to set the objective, manage dependencies, judge the outputs and put everything together. Reading it, I realized our workshop had hit the same wall from the other end. He was looking at execution; we were looking at what happens before execution starts. In both cases, the hard part had moved to the same place: a shared understanding of what we’re building and why. The new bottleneck is context Our final exercise tested exactly that. We called it context portability . Once a team had its brief and task list, they handed one task to a fresh Claude conversation with none of the original discussion. Just the written spec. Could a new AI pick it up and produce something useful? It wasn’t really a test of Claude. It was a test of us. Every gap in the result pointed back to something we hadn’t written down: an assumption that stayed implicit, a decision nobody had actually made, acceptance criteria that only made sense if you’d been in the room. Press enter or click to view image in full size What a fresh Claude can’t understand from the spec alone is exactly what the team never wrote down Anthropic calls the broader discipline [ context engineering ] : managing all the information, instructions and state an AI needs to do good work, rather than just polishing individual prompts. For product teams, I’d add one thing. Good context also has to be honest about its own status. It should clearly separate: what we’ve decided , what we believe , what we still need to learn. That doesn’t mean specifying everything upfront. Discovery is messy and always will be. It means not letting a guess pass for a decision just because it’s written in confident prose. What changes for product teams When execution gets cheap, judgment becomes visible. Humans don’t need to approve every step, but someone has to stay accountable for the direction. That changes what a product brief is for. We used to write it after the thinking was done, as documentation. Now it’s the interface between human judgment and AI execution, and its quality sets the ceiling for everything that follows. We’ve learned to build faster than ever. Now we need to get just as good at deciding what deserves to be built. Because the real risk isn’t that AI will execute poorly. It’s that it will execute brilliantly against the wrong problem. How does your team handle this? Are you investing as much in the quality of your specs and context as in the speed of your AI tooling? I’d love to hear what’s working.
